sections.title: Situation
sections.prompt: What is the board really asking, and what does a week without the incumbent cost?
criteria: Restates the ask as the board's two limits: 24 hours degraded and 90 days to exit
Derives manual onboarding capacity (about 3,086 a week) and the weekly backlog in an outage (about 7,914)
Prices a week of outage (about €3.99M of first-year revenue)
Tiers the four workloads by criticality instead of treating all traffic alike

sections.title: Stakeholders
sections.prompt: Who has a stake, what does each want, and how do you bring them along?
criteria: Covers the board risk committee, the supervisor, the CFO, the CRO and operations, each with a distinct want
Includes the incumbent provider as a party to negotiate with
Shows how the CFO's booked discount and the board's limits can both be met
Ends with one idea that ties the stakeholders together

sections.title: Options
sections.prompt: What are the options, and how does each do on the 24-hour limit, the 90-day exit and the commitment?
criteria: Includes a paper-plan option and shows it fails the 24-hour limit
Checks each option's spend against the €9M commitment
Shows the active-active split misses the commitment and loses most of the discount
Weighs the self-hosted fallback's lower evaluation score, not only its cost

sections.title: Decision and Trade-offs
sections.prompt: What do you recommend, what do you give up, and what would make you revisit it?
criteria: Makes one recommendation that combines the commitment with a live standby for the critical workload
Names what is given up, including the discount lost on moved traffic
Identifies the commitment as the one-way door and routing as reversible
Derives a growth-rate trigger (about 22%) below which the commitment is at risk

sections.title: Economics
sections.prompt: What does each option cost over three years, and how does that compare with an outage?
criteria: Compares three-year totals with the same growth forecast for every option
Separates new spend from engineers already on payroll
Compares the extra cost of readiness with the cost of an outage (about 1.9 days)
Shows year-one new spend against the CFO's budget

sections.title: Org and Ownership
sections.prompt: Who owns the exit plan, the fallbacks and the contract?
criteria: Names one accountable owner
Gives each workload owner their own fallback procedure
Includes second-line challenge from the CRO's team
Has finance tracking the commitment

sections.title: Plan and Milestones
sections.prompt: What happens before the renewal is signed, and how is the plan tested?
criteria: Gets the second provider live and drilled before signing the renewal
Has a gate with a measurable threshold, such as an evaluation score or a switch time
Sets quarterly drills reported to the board
Fits the plan inside the 10-week board date and the 5-month renewal

sections.title: Risk and Governance
sections.prompt: What could make the exit plan fail, and what goes into the contract?
criteria: Keeps live traffic on the standby so it can't degrade unnoticed
Lists exit terms to negotiate, such as termination assistance, version-retirement notice and data deletion, framed as asks or company policy
Keeps one evaluation set run on both providers
Updates the register of third-party arrangements with the tested switch time

sections.title: Metrics
sections.prompt: How do you know the plan works, and what would it hide?
criteria: Pairs each success metric with a guard metric
Measures drill switch time rather than the existence of a plan
Tracks commitment progress next to resilience
Tracks the quality gap between providers

sections.title: Communication
sections.prompt: What does each audience hear, and how often?
criteria: Gives a one-line message for at least four audiences, including the supervisor and the CFO
Tells the CFO the discount depends on the growth forecast
Reports drill results quarterly, including failures
Leads with evidence rather than the plan
